visit_title: After hospital discharge for NSTEMI with drug-eluting stent
follow_up_reason: Two-week post-discharge review after PCI for NSTEMI

clinician_brief.prior_note: Admitted with NSTEMI and treated with percutaneous coronary intervention and a drug-eluting stent to the left anterior descending artery. Discharged two weeks ago on dual antiplatelet therapy and a high-intensity statin.
active_problems: Coronary artery disease status post PCI with drug-eluting stent
previous_plan: Dual antiplatelet therapy for at least twelve months, not to be stopped without cardiology approval
Repeat lipid panel and liver function testing
Return precautions for recurrent chest pain
results_and_observations: Blood pressure today 128/78 mmHg, heart rate 62
No lipid panel yet drawn since discharge
Cardiac rehabilitation intake appointment not yet scheduled
today_tasks: Assess for stent thrombosis and recurrent ischemia red flags
Address statin-associated muscle symptoms without stopping lipid-lowering therapy
Resolve the cost barrier affecting ticagrelor adherence

patient_private.interval_history: Feels generally well and has returned to light activity at home, but has had two episodes of diffuse muscle aching in his thighs since starting the new cholesterol medication.
patient_private.adherence: Stopped the atorvastatin on his own five days ago because of the muscle aches, without telling anyone. Has also skipped his evening ticagrelor dose twice this week because the copay was higher than expected and he was stretching the supply.
patient_private.treatment_response: No chest pain, jaw pain, or shortness of breath since discharge.
patient_private.side_effects: Diffuse thigh muscle aching, worse with stairs, since starting atorvastatin.
patient_private.new_symptoms_and_red_flags: Denies chest pain, chest pressure, exertional dyspnea, palpitations, or syncope.
patient_private.agenda: Wants to know if he can just stay off the cholesterol pill since it is causing him pain.
patient_private.concern: Worried about the cost of his heart medications long term and did not want to bring it up.
patient_private.preference: Wants a plan he can actually afford and stick to.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Untangling two separate self-directed medication gaps two weeks after NSTEMI stenting — statin stopped for myalgia, ticagrelor skipped for cost — and correcting each without abandoning secondary prevention
clinical_knowledge.review_status: guideline-grounded sample; clinician review still recommended before release
core_concepts: Statin-associated muscle symptoms are managed by dose reduction, switching to a different statin, or alternate-day/reduced-frequency dosing — not by outright discontinuation of lipid-lowering therapy, especially this soon after an acute coronary event where high-intensity statin therapy has independent plaque-stabilizing benefit beyond LDL lowering.

Dual antiplatelet therapy interruption in the first weeks after drug-eluting stent placement carries a disproportionately high stent-thrombosis risk compared with later in the treatment course, making his two skipped ticagrelor doses this week a more urgent issue to resolve than the statin question, even though he brought up the statin first.

Medication cost is one of the most common, underreported reasons for post-MI medication nonadherence, and he explicitly avoided raising it — proactively asking about affordability, and connecting patients to generic alternatives or manufacturer/pharmacy assistance programs, is core secondary-prevention practice, not an optional add-on.

Statin myalgia is common and its diagnosis is largely clinical; before assuming a definite statin causal link, it's reasonable to check a creatine kinase if pain is significant, but mild diffuse aching without weakness or dark urine usually does not need extensive workup before trying a practical dose or agent change.

Cardiac rehabilitation after an ACS event is a class I recommendation with mortality benefit; a referral not yet scheduled two weeks out is a gap worth actively closing today rather than assuming it will happen on its own.
diagnostic_clues: No chest pain, jaw pain, dyspnea, or palpitations since discharge is reassuring against an evolving ischemic event today, but does not eliminate his ongoing risk from two missed antiplatelet doses this week.
Diffuse, symmetric thigh muscle aching worse with stairs, without focal weakness, is a pattern typical of statin-associated muscle symptoms rather than a neurologic or vascular cause.
BP 128/78 and HR 62, hemodynamically stable on exam, indicates no acute decompensation today, giving room to focus the visit on medication reconciliation and problem-solving.
No lipid panel drawn since discharge and cardiac rehab not yet scheduled are both process gaps in his post-MI care pathway that this visit should specifically close.
His own statement that he 'did not want to bring up' the cost issue is itself a diagnostic clue — it flags an emotional/financial barrier that needs to be actively drawn out rather than waited for.
common_misconceptions: His framing — wanting to 'just stay off the cholesterol pill' because it hurts — misses that the alternative to stopping is switching, not tolerating pain or going without lipid-lowering therapy altogether after a recent NSTEMI.

Assuming that skipping 'just the evening dose' of ticagrelor here and there is a safe way to stretch a limited supply, when in fact any interruption of dual antiplatelet therapy this early after stenting carries real stent-thrombosis risk regardless of which dose is skipped.

Believing that muscle aches from a new medication are something to quietly self-manage by stopping the drug, rather than something to report, especially when the medication is protecting against a life-threatening recurrent event.
Assuming cost concerns are a personal failing to hide rather than a routine, expected part of post-MI care that his clinical team is equipped and willing to help solve.
dangerous_errors: Reassuring him about the statin muscle symptoms without also addressing the ticagrelor gaps, since the antiplatelet interruption carries the more acute, time-sensitive danger of stent thrombosis.

Restarting atorvastatin at the same dose without acknowledging his myalgia and offering a concrete alternative (lower dose, different statin, or different schedule), risking another self-discontinuation.
Failing to proactively ask about medication cost as a possible explanation for gaps, especially when the patient has signaled reluctance to bring it up himself.
Treating the visit as complete without a specific, dated plan for cardiac rehabilitation enrollment and a repeat lipid panel, leaving both process gaps open indefinitely.
management_principles: Reinforce, clearly and without judgment, that dual antiplatelet therapy must not be stopped or skipped without cardiology input given how recent his drug-eluting stent placement is.
Address the statin-associated muscle symptoms by trialing a lower dose, alternate-day dosing, or a different statin, rather than accepting outright discontinuation of lipid-lowering therapy.

Directly problem-solve the ticagrelor cost barrier — options include checking for a generic/lower-cost P2Y12 inhibitor alternative (with cardiology input), manufacturer assistance programs, or pharmacy discount options.
Confirm and, if needed, actively schedule his cardiac rehabilitation referral and order the overdue lipid panel before he leaves today.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Any switch away from ticagrelor to a different P2Y12 inhibitor after a recent drug-eluting stent should generally involve the treating cardiology team given stent-specific antiplatelet protocols, rather than being changed unilaterally in primary care.

If his muscle symptoms include significant weakness, dark urine, or a substantially elevated creatine kinase, this would raise concern for rhabdomyolysis and needs urgent evaluation rather than routine statin-switch management.

Cost-barrier solutions differ by insurance status and region; what's offered here (assistance programs, generic alternatives) needs to be adapted to his actual coverage and local options rather than assumed universally available.

learning_objectives: Reconcile antiplatelet and statin adherence and identify the reasons for each gap
Explain the danger of stopping dual antiplatelet therapy early after a drug-eluting stent
Address statin-associated muscle symptoms with a dose or agent change rather than outright discontinuation
Screen for recurrent chest pain and other ischemic red flags
Problem-solve the medication cost barrier affecting ticagrelor adherence
Confirm and, if needed, actively arrange the cardiac rehabilitation referral
Agree on a lipid panel recheck and an explicit plan he can afford and follow

reference_soap.subjective: 59M two weeks after PCI with drug-eluting stent for NSTEMI. Self-discontinued atorvastatin five days ago for diffuse thigh myalgia; has skipped two ticagrelor doses this week due to cost. No chest pain, dyspnea, or palpitations. Cardiac rehab not yet scheduled.
reference_soap.objective: BP 128/78, HR 62, hemodynamically stable. No lipid panel drawn since discharge.
reference_soap.assessment: Early self-discontinuation of dual antiplatelet therapy and statin therapy after recent drug-eluting stent placement, driven by a statin side effect and a medication cost barrier.
reference_soap.plan: reinforce that dual antiplatelet therapy must not be stopped without cardiology input given the recent drug-eluting stent, address statin-associated muscle symptoms by trialing a lower dose or an alternative statin rather than stopping lipid-lowering therapy outright, resolve the cost barrier to ticagrelor, confirm cardiac rehabilitation enrollment, and screen for recurrent ischemic symptoms.
